new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress (highest pitch plus greatest intensity, with optional lengthening) falls on the first syllable of the word in more than 88% of the analysed vocabulary; the final syllable has low fading pitch and least intensity, so final vowels devoice or drop. A minority of words carry stress elsewhere (most often the second syllable, occasionally third or fourth), and this location is contrastive: /'yau/ 'dog' vs /ya'u/ 'sun', /'tele/ 'that distant (thing)' vs /te'le/ 'Scrape it!' (p. 63-64), so stress is written phonemically with /'/. Vollrath calls Hewa 'a stress language' with 'regular word stress on the first syllable' (p. 53). Absolute pitch is not distinctive; only the pitch relation of syllables within the word (p. 62).
new_statements.secondary_stress: p. 64: "A secondary Intensity (') may be heard in words of four or more syllables, and falls two syllables behind the one with primary intensity ('). Being predictable, this secondary intensity will not be written phonemically." Same statement at p. 56 (Sec. 3.2.2): "most words of four syllables or longer have a secondary stress which falls on the third syllable when counting the primary stress as the first syllable" - e.g. /'pipalale/ ['pipa,lale] 'a hawk species', /ke'aluapa/ [ke'alu,apa] 'a male name' (p. 64). Vowel length occurs only in a stressed first syllable and is non-phonemic (p. 64).
new_statements.exceptions: p. 64: "Of those words where stress is not on the first syllable, it is more often on the second than on another syllable. Examples of this as well as stress on the third or fourth syllables are given in section 4.3.1." Section 4.3.1 (p. 63) lists patterns S'SS, S'SSS, SS'SS, SS'SSSS, SSS'S (e.g. /ya.pa.'si.na/, /ma.ta.pa.'la/ 'must dispose of (something)'; scanned of the segmentals is unreliable). Minimal pairs by stress position: /'yau/ 'dog' vs /ya'u/ 'sun'; /'sie/ '(I) don't know' vs /si'e/ 'Shoot!'; /'tele/ vs /te'le/; /'matano/ 'bean' vs /ma'tano/ 'must listen' (pp. 63-64). Stress 'occasionally falls on the second vocoid' of a vowel pair, e.g. /kapi'uaa/ 'male name', /u'asi/ 'owner' (p. 56).
new_statements.identity_note: Vollrath 1985 describes Hewa [ham] as analysed by the SIL team (Paul and Karen Vollrath) from their own field data; the scanned pages (printed 52-73) name no dialect or village. No other variety is described.

new_statements.relation_note: Catalog (StressTyp2 'StressTyp2') codes Hewa as initial stress (initial stress). The OPD is compatible: initial is the unmarked/default position (only non-initial stress is written). It adds that stress placement is lexically contrastive in a minority of words (three minimal pairs given), which the plain fixed: initial syllable coding does not record. Consistent with Vollrath 1985 (same author, held by the project): 'Regular word stress on the first syllable', 'more than 88% of the words have that syllable first', non-initial stress 'more often on the second'.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is on the first syllable by default: the practical orthography leaves initial stress unmarked and writes an acute accent only when stress falls on a non-initial syllable. Stress position is nonetheless contrastive in some lexical items, shown by stress minimal pairs (mátanö 'bean' vs matánö 'must listen', téle vs telé, áföle vs af´öle); no tone or length contrast is illustrated under the 'tone, stress, length' heading, only stress placement.
new_statements.secondary_stress: Nothing said in the OPD (the author's 1985 'Hewa Phonemes' paper, already held by the project but not a listed work here, describes a predictable secondary intensity two syllables after the primary).
new_statements.exceptions: Lexical items with non-initial (mostly second-syllable) stress exist and contrast minimally with initial-stressed words: matánö 'must listen', telé 'scrape it!', af´öle 'where?'; in the orthographic text sample such a word is written Ma'tanö. Unstressed final vowels (especially /i/ and a second vowel whose symbol did not extract) tend to be dropped.
new_statements.identity_note: The OPD covers the Hewa language [HAM] of Lake Kopiago (Southern Highlands), Porgera (Enga) and Oksapmin (Sandaun) areas, villages Atini, Wisiki, Wanakipe, Waiki, Malieni, Papakuke, Fölini, Teki (Sisimin); no particular dialect is singled out.

audit.recode_to: fixed-dominant (strict set OUT, code 'lexical'; dominant rule unchanged: initial, initial stress, no change to window). Reason: the held, page-verified deciding source itself states stress is phonemic - Vollrath 1985:63 'some words contrast only on the basis of which syllable carries both the greater intensity and highest pitch.. symbolised by /ˈ/ phonemically', >88% (not all) words initial, minimal pairs and non-initial forms in native nouns and verbs (pp.63-64), and Cochran 1968 fn.5 independently writes 'Phonemic stress'. Under our scope rules sec. 2 ('a source stating stress is contrastive' = sufficient evidence for OUT-code lexical) and the Juma precedent (predominant pattern + contrastive residue in native vocabulary -> outside the strict set lexical, in the dominant set), Hewa fails IN-test 1 at strict set. The catalog's own domain check already carries lexical_stress='yes' and the note 'majority rule, not exceptionless', yet not in the strict set / 'verified-clean' stands in the current catalog and V5_CANDIDATE.

audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: both deciding sentences found verbatim in the scanned text we hold at the cited lines and confirmed on rendered page images of printed pp.63-64 (scanned '88X' = '88%'). (2) Deciding source: a 1985 SIL phonemic statement, the fullest phonology Glottolog knows for Hewa (3 descriptive refs total); Cochran 1968 (held) agrees stress is phonemic; the only unheld later item is a 4-page 1992 OPD by the same author. So the source base is the best available and is. (3) The problem is not the source but the register: the same pages that supply the 'normally first syllable / 88%' quote also state explicitly that stress placement is contrastive and is written phonemically, with minimal pairs among native nouns and verbs and c.12% non-initial words. That is the catalog's own sufficient evidence for strict-register exclusion (lexical), exactly parallel to the Juma ruling; the dominant-regist
